transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-05-03
- Start: 16:00 PDT
- Duration: ~75 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Karen Liu (Aurelia Head of ML), Derek Soto (Aurelia Infra), Priya Nair (Aurelia PM)

Summary:
Short scoping for a pilot focused on latency acceptance (TTFT vs TPOT trade-offs), traffic sizing, and a benchmarking ramp plan. Customer needs p95 and p99 commitments for a production chat assistant used in clinical scheduling with bursty traffic spikes. Discussed measurement methodology, sampling, and what constitutes "pass" for the pilot.

Topics discussed:
- Definition of TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total-per-token) and which map to user experience for Aurelia
- Sampling strategy (when to measure p95/p99, sample sizes) and traffic synthesis for burstiness
- Benchmark orchestration: model variants, quantization, caching and fallbacks
- Ramp schedule and acceptance criteria for pilot handoff
- Security/compliance: SOC2, data retention, private routing concerns

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, um we'll run about an hour, maybe 75 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:08] Karen Liu: hi yeah Karen, head of ML at Aurelia, thanks. we've got Derek on infra and Priya product.
[00:12] Derek Soto: Derek here.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Priya.
[00:15] Maya Chen: great. Ravi and I from Redwood will run the technical scope portion — Ravi will do the emulation/measurement bit.
[00:21] Ravi Patel: hi all, quick note, I'll mention the traffic harness and the measurement script we usually use — it's lightweight, hooks KV cache priming and simulates prefix reuse.
[00:31] Karen Liu: awesome, the high level we care about is responsiveness for patients scheduling, so perceived snappiness matters more than per-token cost for now, but cost matters long term. we want p95 under 600ms for TTFT ideally and p99 under 1.2s, that's our starting ask.
[00:47] Maya Chen: okay that's helpful. quick framing: TTFT is what the user sees as the app's response start; TPOT is total time to finish the whole answer. For chat UIs TTFT often drives perceived latency, but TPOT matters for longer responses and downstream timeouts.
[01:05] Karen Liu: yes exactly. some of our actions are short single-sentence replies and some are multi-step confirmations. we probably need mixed SLOs.
[01:14] Ravi Patel: totally. For mixed workloads we recommend dual SLOs: a TTFT p95 target and a TPOT p99 target. Also sample by endpoint and by prompt class — top 10 prompts should be separately measured.
[01:28] Priya Nair: can you explain sampling sizes? like how many requests do you need to estimate p99 robustly?
[01:32] Ravi Patel: good question. p99 needs more samples — statistically you'd want tens of thousands of samples ideally across your distribution but for a pilot we use stratified sampling: capture 10k samples per prompt class if possible, or at least 50k global samples across the run. we'll also do bootstrap confidence intervals.
[01:50] Karen Liu: 50k sounds heavy, what's the typical run time?
[01:54] Ravi Patel: depends on your qps. if you run a 200 qps synthetic run, 50k samples is ~250s, five minutes. but you need to sweep load shapes — steady, ramp, and burst.
[02:10] Derek Soto: network comes into play; our VPC peering adds a small RTT. we need to account for that in baseline numbers. can you separate service-side inference latency from network egress?
[02:20] Maya Chen: yes, we'll instrument client- and server-side timing. the harness records request time, time-to-first-byte, first-token event, and final token. we can provide both delta-inference (server-only) and end-to-end numbers.
[02:34] Priya Nair: for acceptance criteria do we need both pass/fail and a grey area?
[02:38] Maya Chen: we usually define a pass band and a watch band. e.g., TTFT p95 <= 600ms is pass, 600–800ms is watch (needs mitigation), >800ms fail. TPOT p99 <= 1.2s pass, 1.2–1.8s watch, >1.8s fail. those are examples — we can tune.
[02:56] Karen Liu: that matches our instincts. how do you handle tokenization variance? our prompts vary a lot.
[03:02] Ravi Patel: we normalize by measuring token counts and stratifying; also we score by effective sequence length. quantization affects TPOT more than TTFT in some models due to decode speed, so we'll test both FP16 and int8 variants.
[03:16] Derek Soto: fallbacks—if the dedicated pool is saturated what's the behavior? we need graceful degradation.
[03:21] Maya Chen: Redwood supports model fallbacks and routing policies. the plan for pilot is to pin a primary model then configure a lower-capacity variant as fallback. we'll capture latency on fallback as a separate label in the reports.
[03:33] Priya Nair: can you also measure tail at p999? clinicians care about worst-case sometimes.
[03:38] Ravi Patel: p999 is noisy without lots of samples; we can include it but treat it as advisory unless you run large-scale sweeps. for pilot acceptance we stick to p99.
[03:48] Karen Liu: sample collection — do we need to sanitize PII? our prompts include patient names.
[03:53] Maya Chen: for the pilot you can provide synthetic or redacted prompts. Redwood's hosted logs can be configured not to retain full prompts; for Private deployments you keep everything on-prem. we'll share our data handling docs.
[04:06] Derek Soto: network egress costs too — if we do frequent benchmarking it could add up.
[04:10] Maya Chen: noted, we'll scope frequency. initial runs can be in a dedicated test window to limit egress.
[04:16] Ravi Patel: on measurement harness specifics: we'll run three sweep shapes — steady-state at nominal qps, a controlled ramp from 0 to 2x over 10 minutes, and a burst test (short 30s spikes at 5x). We'll capture TTFT, TPOT, tail latencies, and compute p50/p90/p95/p99 per shape and per prompt class.
[04:39] Priya Nair: sounds good. timeline wise, when can you deliver the initial results?
[04:42] Maya Chen: if we get your traffic profile by Friday (2027-05-07) Ravi can ship the initial harness by Monday the 10th and we can schedule the first run the week of the 17th pending peering.
[04:53] Karen Liu: dev deadlines align. I want to flag success criteria beyond latency: throughput—sustained qps with error rate <0.5% is a hard requirement.
[05:02] Ravi Patel: we'll include error-rate thresholds and token-error metrics. we'll instrument model-side errors, timeouts, and 5xx.
[05:09] Derek Soto: for the private deployment option, what's the typical lead time?
[05:12] Maya Chen: Private installs are longer — normally 6–8 weeks for on-prem or VPC private control plane. for pilot we recommend starting on hosted or dedicated reserved capacity and migrating to private if needed.
[05:24] Karen Liu: any differences in latency between hosted and dedicated?
[05:27] Ravi Patel: dedicated gives you more predictable latency because of reserved GPUs and isolation. hosted is fine for initial tests but you might see more variance during noisy neighbor situations. our benchmark reports always include a predictability score.
[05:40] Priya Nair: on the measurement output format, can we get a CSV plus a short dashboard?
[05:44] Maya Chen: yes, we provide raw CSVs with labeled events and a summary PDF. we also deliver a small open dashboard that shows per-shape and per-prompt SLO curves.
[05:54] Karen Liu: want to dig into prompt classes — top 10 by frequency then a long-tail sample set?
[05:59] Ravi Patel: exactly. we'll take your top 10 by frequency (you provide), and then sample 1k random prompts from the long tail for exploratory checks. the acceptance will be based on top-10, long-tail is advisory.
[06:12] Derek Soto: instrumentation: do you require agents on our side or can you run the harness remotely?
[06:16] Ravi Patel: the harness can run from either side. for network fidelity we prefer running a local agent in your infra that hits the Redwood endpoint to capture realistic RTTs; we also can run from our test VMs to control the baseline.
[06:29] Priya Nair: regression detection — how do you ensure we don't degrade quality when we optimize for latency?
[06:34] Maya Chen: we include a set of golden prompts and quality checks — we run an eval that computes semantic similarity and surface-level checks; if quality regresses beyond your threshold the run is flagged.
[06:45] Karen Liu: what's the cost implication of quantization? we want latency but not big quality drops.
[06:50] Ravi Patel: we run quantization profiles and compute acceptance on both latency and quality. often int8 gives 20–40% latency wins with small quality loss; we'll surface those trade-offs.
[06:59] Priya Nair: can you show an example acceptance clause?
[07:02] Maya Chen: example: TTFT p95 <= 600ms and TPOT p99 <= 1.2s on the top-10 prompt set under nominal load (X qps). Quality: semantic similarity >= 0.92 on golden prompts. Error rate < 0.5%. If two of three conditions fail we flag as fail.
[07:22] Derek Soto: let's talk about ramping to production. if pilot passes, what's a recommended rollout?
[07:26] Ravi Patel: a staged rollout: canary at 5% traffic for 24–48h, then 25% for 48–72h, then 100% if stable. We'll collect SLO metrics at each stage and run automated rollback if p99 exceeds watch band.
[07:41] Karen Liu: SLA expectations — do you offer SLA for Dedicated?
[07:45] Maya Chen: yes Dedicated includes SLA-backed latency and availability depending on the contract tier. we'll share the SLA terms.
[07:51] Priya Nair: security — SSO and audit logs?
[07:54] Maya Chen: SAML SSO and RBAC supported, audit logs available; we can also route logs to your logging endpoint. we'll attach the security checklist to the follow-up.
[08:05] Karen Liu: one operational note: our peak days show sudden 10x spikes for ~60s due to campaign blasts, so burst handling is critical.
[08:13] Ravi Patel: that's why we'll run short high-intensity bursts and observe queueing/backpressure and any dropped requests. we'll also test prefix caching effectiveness since many prompts share common prefixes.
[08:26] Priya Nair: is prefix caching something you can tune during pilot?
[08:29] Ravi Patel: yes, caching parameters (TTL, prefix match sensitivity) can be tuned. We can also try a KV cache priming phase prior to spike windows.
[08:41] Maya Chen: ok let's quickly align on timeline and owners: you provide traffic profile by Friday, Redwood provides harness Mon, run week of 17th, follow-up report within 3 business days. Does that work?
[08:51] Karen Liu: yes that works.
[08:52] Derek Soto: fine.
[08:53] Priya Nair: ok.
[08:54] Maya Chen: any other questions?
[08:56] Karen Liu: how do you measure warm vs cold starts for long-tail prompts?
[08:59] Ravi Patel: we measure warm (after KV cache priming) and cold separately. cold starts will be labeled and excluded from pass criteria unless you want to include them.
[09:09] Priya Nair: what about concurrency limits per connection?
[09:12] Ravi Patel: we'll model realistic connection counts; our harness supports many workers and multiplexed HTTP/2 connections to reflect your client behaviour.
[09:21] Maya Chen: ok we'll capture all this in the benchmark template. we'll also share a short checklist for pre-run items (peering, credentials, sample prompts, golden set).
[09:30] Karen Liu: last question on metrics: do you compute cost per 1k responses alongside latency?
[09:34] Maya Chen: yes we provide cost estimates for each configuration and show latency vs cost tradeoff curves.
[09:40] Priya Nair: great. thanks everyone.
[09:43] Maya Chen: recap of next steps — Maya will share the template and SOC2 extract, Ravi will ship the harness and traffic script, Karen will send top-10 prompts and traffic sketch. schedule slot week of 17th.
[09:56] Karen Liu: thanks all.
[09:57] Derek Soto: thanks.
[09:58] Priya Nair: bye.
